title: Rethinking Legal Education in the AI Era (AI Strategy Statement)
author: University of Chicago Law School

dom.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source supports adapting legal education in response to AI while preserving rigor, but it does not address whether AI will restructure rather than eliminate legal jobs, whether broad displacement is occurring, or whether junior pipelines face the sharpest workforce risk.
qs: It is thus critical for us to use this moment to carefully reflect on how legal education should adapt.
With AI disrupting higher education, our commitment to rigorous legal education also must mean openness to even rapid adaptation.

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The source accepts the need to combine AI-enabled practice with independent legal reasoning and materially develops that proposition through a differentiated curriculum: protected effortful learning for first-year students, adaptable rather than product-specific AI skills, optional advanced experimentation, and hybrid writing assessment designed to preserve sustained independent work.
qs: The feedback we have received throughout this process has been consistent: We need to ensure that our students actually learn to think critically, strategically, and independently without relying on AI; but we also must face the reality that AI tools are already widely available to our students, and our graduates will be expected to be prepared to use them in legal practice.
Thus, we are developing an approach that introduces elements of AI-resilient design while sustaining the project of training students to undertake ambitious and independent writing projects.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Chicago accepts the cluster’s core framing that legal education must develop independent judgment and AI competence together, then materially develops it through a staged, course-specific model: restrictive foundational conditions, combined unaided and supervised AI writing practice, experimentation in electives, supervised clinical use, and revisable governance. Its proposals support the synthesis’s timing and assessment distinctions, while remaining institutional plans rather than measured evidence of educational effectiveness.
qs: The feedback we have received throughout this process has been consistent: We need to ensure that our students actually learn to think critically, strategically, and independently without relying on AI; but we also must face the reality that AI tools are already widely available to our students, and our graduates will be expected to be prepared to use them in legal practice.
Throughout the year, students will write without AI, while also using AI for research, revision, iterating on drafts, and preparation for oral argument.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: Chicago accepts that AI exposure alone does not create professional readiness and materially develops the proposition through a staged curriculum: independent reasoning and unaided writing form the foundation, while supervised AI use and joint review build the capacity to assess and improve AI output. Its contribution is a revisable institutional strategy and pilot, not demonstrated learning-outcome evidence.
qs: The feedback we have received throughout this process has been consistent: We need to ensure that our students actually learn to think critically, strategically, and independently without relying on AI; but we also must face the reality that AI tools are already widely available to our students, and our graduates will be expected to be prepared to use them in legal practice.
Our approach will treat writing *without *AI as the foundation and will layer writing *with *AI onto it.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: Chicago accepts the cluster’s balance between independent reasoning and supervised AI competence, then develops it into a concrete staged model: unaided writing as the foundation, layered AI-assisted work, joint review, protected first-year learning and later experimentation. Its plans substantively extend the proposition, although they remain pilots rather than evidence of measured educational outcomes.
qs: Our approach will treat writing *without *AI as the foundation and will layer writing *with *AI onto it.
In this way, students will develop their own writing skills independent of generative AI tools while also developing their ability to supervise AI and critique its output.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The strategy accepts the cluster’s core view that AI should augment rather than displace human legal judgment and that uncritical reliance creates competence risks. It materially extends the proposition with a concrete educational model: preserve unaided writing as a foundation, teach students to supervise and critique AI output, use practice-specific safeguards, and continually revise policies as tools and practice evolve.
qs: In this way, students will develop their own writing skills independent of generative AI tools while also developing their ability to supervise AI and critique its output.
Thus, all the changes we are currently making will be subject to review, reconsideration, and revision as we learn more and as both technology and the practice of law evolve.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The statement accepts selective, human-supervised deployment and materially extends the cluster by translating it into a legal-education operating model: students gain real-client experience both with and without AI, while clinics adopt practice-specific safeguards against AI-created errors. Its iterative policy review also aligns with continuous, use-context-specific governance.
qs: As these tools and policies are implemented, the goal is to ensure that all students in clinics are working both with AI and without AI for real clients in real practice settings.

Further, the clinics are each developing their own policies, tailored to their practice areas, for appropriate use of AI and to safeguard against AI-created errors in court filings and other work product.

kp.k: Legal education must preserve independence while preparing AI users
kp.d: The Law School reports consistent feedback from consultations with alumni, law firm and business leaders, legal technology executives, associates, faculty, staff and students: graduates need both independent reasoning skills and readiness to use AI in practice. Its strategy draws on these consultations, institutional experience and a survey of emerging literature, rather than presenting a quantified empirical study.
qs: We need to ensure that our students actually learn to think critically, strategically, and independently without relying on AI; but we also must face the reality that AI tools are already widely available to our students, and our graduates will be expected to be prepared to use them in legal practice.

kp.k: AI resilience means protecting learning, not banning AI
kp.d: The statement recommends designing instruction and assessment to require sustained intellectual effort and discourage outsourcing learning to AI. It distinguishes shortcuts that undermine professional judgment from uses that increase engagement, such as clarifying background concepts and generating practice problems.
qs: We thus need to ensure that our students do not rely on AI-provided shortcuts that help them produce easy answers but stunt intellectual growth.

This requires developing AI-resilient pedagogy, by which we mean modes of classroom interaction and performance evaluation that reward students’ effortful and sustained engagement with the material, and discourage the offloading of work to AI tools.

kp.k: Human judgment and relationships remain anticipated professional differentiators
kp.d: The Law School predicts that oral advocacy, strategic judgment, critical thinking and relationships with clients and stakeholders are likely to remain human responsibilities, partly because clients, employers, judges and society will want humans to perform them. It acknowledges AI assistance in these tasks while recommending renewed emphasis on the human skills involved; this is an expectation, not a demonstrated boundary of automation.
qs: Second, AI may transform the legal profession, but many aspects of legal practice are likely to remain the domain of humans, not merely because humans are good at them, but because clients, employers, judges, and society will want humans to perform them.
Among others, these aspects of legal practice are likely to include oral advocacy, strategic judgment, critical thinking, and developing and maintaining relationships with clients and stakeholders.

kp.k: Durable AI education requires adaptability beyond current tools
kp.d: The statement asserts that AI is already pervasive in legal practice and predicts further adoption. Because present tools and techniques may become obsolete before students enter practice, it recommends analytical and theoretical preparation for responsible, effective and ethical use across technological changes, rather than merely teaching current software.
qs: Third, AI is already a pervasive part of legal practice and will become more so.
But legal technology is changing rapidly, and there is no guarantee that the specific AI tools or techniques that are ascendant today will be useful when current students enter practice.
Law schools must give students the analytical skills and theoretical toolkit to adapt as technologies change.

kp.k: Core first-year courses will pilot coordinated device restrictions
kp.d: For 2026–2027, the Law School will pilot classroom device prohibitions and in-class examinations without internet, electronic files or apps across all required 1L core sections, retaining Socratic teaching. Exceptions include designated note-taking scribes, authorized technology-enabled activities and disability accommodations. Its rationale is that foundational struggle matters especially when students are least equipped to judge AI output; it invokes institutional experience and an emerging scholarly consensus on active, in-person learning without supplying study details.
qs: Student expertise at judging the quality of AI output is at its nadir.
We will be piloting a coordinated approach to classroom and examination policies for the core 1L curriculum during the 2026–2027 academic year.
Across all 1L sections, we will prohibit the use of electronic devices such as laptops, tablets, and phones in the classroom.
Additionally, examinations will be in-class without access to the internet, electronic files, or apps.

kp.k: First-year writing combines independent drafting and supervised AI use
kp.d: A separate 2026–2027 legal research and writing pilot responds to the expectation that many, possibly most, students will use AI during their 1L summer employment. Independent writing remains foundational, alongside AI-assisted research, revision, draft iteration and oral-argument preparation. Joint instructor-student review is intended to develop writing ability and the human work of checking, improving and supervising AI output.
qs: Many (if not most) students will spend their 1L summers in professional environments where they will be expected to use AI tools for research and writing tasks.
Throughout the year, students will write without AI, while also using AI for research, revision, iterating on drafts, and preparation for oral argument.
Students and their instructors will review together both their writing and their use of AI.
In this way, students will develop their own writing skills independent of generative AI tools while also developing their ability to supervise AI and critique its output.

kp.k: Electives permit experimentation and optional deeper AI specialization
kp.d: Upper-level courses and spring 1L electives retain Socratic teaching, device restrictions and no-access in-class exams as defaults rather than mandates. The school encourages formative assessment, group projects, oral presentations, peer feedback and AI-supported study tools. Courses on AI use and tool creation remain elective, with further expansion planned; cross-listed and other-unit courses may follow different policies.
qs: For these courses, the use of the Socratic Method, no-device policies, and in-class, no-access exams will remain, but as default rules rather than required policies.
Our faculty have already begun experimenting with tools such as custom chatbots that serve as study aids, AI-generated practice problems, and the like.
These courses are all offered as electives, so that students can select how many AI-focused classes, and which of these classes, they wish to take.
We plan to continue to grow our upper-level offerings on AI.

kp.k: AI-generated papers challenge writing's role in professional formation
kp.d: The statement argues that AI can produce substantial, plausible academic papers without the human effort that makes writing educational. Although supervised classroom writing can establish original effort, it would sacrifice sustained independent work over longer periods. The school therefore seeks to preserve ambitious writing projects while adding AI-resilient elements and encouraging experimentation with workshops, presentations, supervised writing and discussions.
qs: Yet the primary modes of writing in the upper-level curriculum—research papers and reaction papers—are under stress in a world in which AI can produce plausible and substantial academic papers without the kind of human input that paper-writing is intended to involve.
Yet such requirements lose an important aspect of the exercise of writing, which is sustained and independent effort across hours, days, and weeks to create a significant piece of work.

kp.k: Research papers will require in-person oral discussion
kp.d: Beginning with the statement's class of rising 2Ls, the JD substantial research paper requirement adds an in-person discussion with the supervising professor after submission of a complete draft or final paper. Individual discussion or workshop-style presentation must probe reasoning and implications. The stated purposes are to test students' own understanding without technology and train real-time explanation and defense of ideas for courtrooms, negotiations, client counseling and collaboration.
qs: We will be adding one additional requirement, which is that all students will be required to engage in an oral discussion of their SRP with their supervising professor, in an in-person setting.
This discussion will occur after a complete draft (or final version) of the paper has been submitted to the professor.
Either way, the oral exchange will involve the student answering questions that probe the reasoning of the paper and the implications of its arguments.
First, this requirement makes the SRP more AI-resilient by providing a test of a student’s thinking about what they have written in a setting where they cannot lean on technology.

kp.k: Clinics combine supervised AI practice and human lawyering
kp.d: The school predicts that client expectations will increase pressure for immediate graduate competence in AI use, making clinics an important supervised preparation setting. It reports obtaining general-purpose legal AI and tools for transactional work, immigration and discovery, with further procurement underway. Clinics are developing practice-specific policies to prevent AI-created errors in filings and other work, with a goal of every clinic student serving real clients both with and without AI while developing advocacy, relationships and strategy.
qs: Client needs and expectations will create pressure for graduates to be able to immediately use AI responsibly, effectively, and ethically.
As a practical matter, this means that for many graduates, law school clinics are the best opportunity to receive close and careful supervision of their use of AI tools.

Further, the clinics are each developing their own policies, tailored to their practice areas, for appropriate use of AI and to safeguard against AI-created errors in court filings and other work product.
As these tools and policies are implemented, the goal is to ensure that all students in clinics are working both with AI and without AI for real clients in real practice settings.

kp.k: Existing infrastructure supports tool access and access-to-justice education
kp.d: The school reports forming an AI committee in early 2023 after ChatGPT's public release at the end of 2022. Subsequent measures include policies and guidance, a first-year AI module, upper-level AI courses, an AI Lab teaching tool development for access to justice, and licenses providing students, faculty and staff with tools used in practice. These are reported institutional activities, not evidence of improved learning or access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: Our law school formed an AI committee in early 2023 and began releasing policies and guidance on the use of AI.

Since then, we have added an AI module into our first-year legal research and writing program, introduced several upper-level courses on AI and the law, founded an AI Lab to teach our students how to develop AI tools to help improve access to justice, and negotiated licenses with leading AI companies so that our students, faculty, and staff have access to the resources used by practicing lawyers.

kp.k: AI policies require transparency and ongoing revision
kp.d: Instructors must explain AI policies in syllabi and in class. The school commits to monitoring practice through employers and alumni, securing relevant tools through technology firms, sharing faculty experience and reconsidering policies with faculty, student and alumni input. It explicitly treats the strategy and current changes as provisional because technology and legal practice are evolving rapidly.
qs: To that end, each instructor must state their AI policy explicitly in the course syllabus and describe the policy in class.
We recognize that no statement of an AI strategy or vision can be final.
Thus, all the changes we are currently making will be subject to review, reconsideration, and revision as we learn more and as both technology and the practice of law evolve.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The University of Chicago Law School presents AI as an established and growing feature of legal practice that requires both AI competence and preservation of independent human judgment.
pts.d: The institutional statement claims that AI is already pervasive in legal practice and predicts further adoption, with graduates expected to use it professionally. It predicts that oral advocacy, strategic judgment, critical thinking, and relationships will likely remain human responsibilities, partly because clients, employers, judges, and society want humans to perform them, while acknowledging AI assistance in these activities. Rapid technological change means training must develop adaptable analytical capabilities rather than proficiency only in current tools. In legal education, the statement claims that AI shortcuts can stunt intellectual growth and that AI-generated academic papers threaten traditional writing assignments, while also recognizing opportunities for AI-supported study and assessment. Its proposed response combines independent writing and reasoning with supervised AI use, critique of outputs, and more AI-resilient assessment. It also predicts that clinical education will become more important as clients expect graduates to use AI competently. These are institutional claims and educational rationales, not reported findings of measured changes in lawyer employment or legal-market economics.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The statement grounds its position in stakeholder consultation, institutional experience, and an unspecified review of scholarship and professional literature.
pts.d: The Law School reports consultations with alumni, law-firm leaders and associates, business leaders, legal-technology executives, faculty, staff, and students. It characterizes the feedback as consistently supporting both independent thinking and readiness to use AI in practice. It also cites three years of institutional experience and a review of emerging literature. Reported activities—including an AI committee, an AI module in first-year legal research and writing, AI electives, an access-to-justice AI Lab, tool licensing, and faculty experimentation—provide implementation experience rather than measured evidence of effectiveness. Its preference for active, in-person learning is attributed to experience and an emerging scholarly consensus. The document provides no named empirical studies, quantitative adoption estimates, benchmarks, or measured learning outcomes supporting its broader predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The July 9, 2026 statement distinguishes current AI use from open-ended predictions and schedules major first-year curriculum pilots for 2026–2027.
pts.d: AI's prevalence is presented as current; further adoption and continued human responsibility are predictions without a fixed endpoint. The latter is explicitly qualified as likely and does not exclude AI assistance. The statement anticipates professional AI use as early as students' first-year summers and seeks output-review skills by the end of the first year. It warns that current tools may not remain useful when students enter practice. Coordinated first-year core-course policies and a revised legal research and writing curriculum are pilots for the 2026–2027 academic year. The substantial research paper oral-discussion requirement begins with the then-rising second-year class. AI-resilient teaching is expressly not a prohibition on all AI use: independent foundational work is combined with appropriate AI-supported learning. Policies vary by curricular stage and clinical practice area, and all changes remain subject to revision as technology and practice evolve.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law students, graduates, educators, employers, and clients; the emphasis is on competence, supervision, and professional relationships rather than market displacement.
pts.d: First-year students are described as particularly inexperienced at judging AI output and therefore in need of independent foundational learning and supervised AI training. Upper-level students face more varied teaching methods and an oral defense of their substantial research papers. Graduates face employer and client expectations of immediate responsible AI use. Faculty and clinical instructors must adapt teaching, assessment, supervision, and practice-specific safeguards against AI-created errors. Clients, courts, counterparties, and other stakeholders are affected by the quality of AI-assisted work and the continued need for human advocacy, judgment, and relationships. Clinics are identified as important settings for supervised use on real matters, including transactional work, immigration, and litigation discovery. The AI Lab's access-to-justice purpose is reported, but the statement does not claim a measured reduction in unmet legal need. It does not forecast changes in staffing ratios, fees, firm market shares, or job numbers.
